question_en: Which OOP feature is summed up by the phrase "one interface, many forms"?
explanation_en: Polymorphism (Greek: many forms) lets one name or interface stand for different behaviours, for example one method name with several implementations. Encapsulation bundles data with methods, and inheritance lets a class reuse another class's members.

Every constructor first calls its superclass constructor (an implicit super() call). new C() calls B(), which calls A(). A() prints A, then control returns and B() prints B, then C() prints C. Output: ABC.

question_en: Binding data and the methods that work on that data into a single unit (a class) is called:
explanation_en: Encapsulation wraps data members and member functions together in a class and usually hides the data behind private access. This protects the data from direct outside access.

Creating d runs the base constructor first (B), then the derived constructor (D). When d goes out of scope at the end of main, destructors run in the reverse order: ~Derived prints ~D, then ~Base prints ~B. Output: B D ~D ~B.

Overloading is resolved at compile time by choosing the most specific method. byte has no exact match, so it widens to int, the closest type: int. 5L is a long: long. 5.0f is a float with no float version, so it widens to double: double. Output: int long double.

question_en: Which of the following operators CANNOT be overloaded in C++?
explanation_en: C++ does not allow overloading of :: (scope resolution), . (member access), .* (pointer-to-member), ?: (conditional) and sizeof. Operators such as +, [] and << can be overloaded; << is commonly overloaded for output with cout.
The reference a has type Animal but points to a Dog object. Java instance methods are bound at run time (dynamic method dispatch), so the overriding Dog.sound() runs. Output: Bark.

question_en: Which statement about a friend function of a class in C++ is TRUE?

options.en: It is not a member but can access the class's private members
It is a member function that can access only public members
It is automatically inherited by all derived classes
It must be called through an object using the dot operator

explanation_en: A friend function is declared inside the class with the keyword friend but is not a member of the class. It can still access the class's private and protected members. It is called like an ordinary function, and friendship is not inherited.

Only instance methods are overridden and chosen at run time. Fields and static methods are chosen by the reference type at compile time. The reference type is P, so obj.x is 10 and obj.s() is "P"; obj.m() runs Q's version and gives "Q". 10 + "P" + "Q" = "10PQ".

question_en: Method overloading in Java is an example of:
explanation_en: In overloading, methods share a name but differ in their parameter lists, and the compiler picks the version from the argument types. That is compile-time polymorphism. Overriding is resolved at run time (dynamic method dispatch).

p is a Shape* pointing to a Circle. name() is not virtual, so the call is bound at compile time by the pointer type: Shape::name() prints Shape. area() is virtual, so the call is bound at run time by the object type: Circle::area() prints CircleArea. Output: Shape CircleArea.

question_en: Which statement about Java interfaces (Java 8 and later) is TRUE?

options.en: An interface can have non-final instance variables
An interface can declare a public constructor
An interface can have default and static methods with a body
A class can implement only one interface at a time

explanation_en: Since Java 8 an interface may contain default and static methods with bodies (and private methods since Java 9). Interface fields are always public static final, interfaces have no constructors, and a class may implement many interfaces.

subtopic: static member shared by all objects
explanation_en: count is static, so all objects share one copy. id is an instance variable, so each object has its own copy. a: count=1, id=1; b: count=2, id=2; c: count=3, id=3. Printing a.id, b.id and Counter.count gives 1 2 3.

question_en: Which statement about the final keyword in Java is FALSE?

options.en: A final method can be overridden in a subclass
A final class cannot be extended by another class
A final variable can be assigned a value only once
A blank final variable can be assigned in the constructor

explanation_en: A final method cannot be overridden, so that statement is false. A final class cannot be subclassed (for example String), and a final variable gets its value exactly once. A blank final instance variable can be given its value in a constructor.

this(...) must be the first statement, so each constructor calls the next before printing. Box() calls Box(5), which calls Box(5, 5). Box(5, 5) sets w = h = 5 and prints WH; control then returns to print S, then D. b.w * b.h = 25, so the output is WHSD 25.

question_en: Arrange the Java access levels from MOST restrictive to LEAST restrictive.
explanation_en: private allows access only inside the class. Default (package-private, no keyword) adds the same package. protected adds subclasses in other packages. public allows access from everywhere. So the order is private > default > protected > public.

subtopic: super method call in multilevel inheritance
explanation_en: The object is a SportsCar, so SportsCar.type() runs. It returns "Sports-" + super.type(), where super refers to Car. Car.type() returns "Car-" + Vehicle.type(), which is "Car-Vehicle". Result: Sports-Car-Vehicle.

question_en: In C++, which access specifier makes a base-class member accessible in its derived classes but not to unrelated outside code?
explanation_en: A protected member can be used inside the class and inside classes derived from it, but not by unrelated code. A private member is not accessible even in derived classes, and a public member is accessible everywhere. virtual is not an access specifier.

subtopic: Integer caching and == with wrapper classes
explanation_en: Autoboxing uses Integer.valueOf(), which returns cached objects for values from -128 to 127. a and b refer to the same cached object, so a == b is true. 200 is outside the cache, so c and d are different objects and c == d is false. equals() compares the values: true.

question_en: Which type of inheritance is NOT supported in Java through classes?
explanation_en: A Java class can extend only one class, so multiple inheritance of classes is not allowed. This avoids the diamond problem. A class can still implement several interfaces, which gives multiple inheritance of type.

subtopic: Static block, instance block and constructor order
explanation_en: A static block runs once, when the class is loaded, before the first object is created: S. For every object, the instance initializer block runs before the constructor body: I then C. Two objects give S + IC + IC = SICIC.

question_en: Which statement correctly describes how the JDK, JRE and JVM are related?

options.en: The JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM
The JVM contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JDK
The JRE contains the JDK, and the JDK contains the JVM
The JDK and the JRE do not use the JVM at all

explanation_en: The JVM executes bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the core class libraries needed to run programs. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, javadoc and jar. So JDK > JRE > JVM.

An abstract class cannot be instantiated, but it can have a constructor, which runs when a subclass object is created. new Square(3) first runs Shape() (prints Shape), then the Square body (prints Square). area() returns the double 3.0 * 3.0, which prints as 9.0.

question_en: The Java compiler (javac) translates a .java source file into:

options.en: Native machine code in an .exe file

explanation_en: javac produces platform-independent bytecode in .class files. The JVM on any platform then interprets this bytecode or JIT-compiles it. This is the basis of "write once, run anywhere".

null can be passed to both versions. Java then chooses the most specific method, and String is more specific than Object because String is a subclass of Object. So f(String) is called and prints String. There is no ambiguity, so the code compiles.

question_en: In the Java ClassLoader delegation hierarchy, which class loader has NO parent class loader?
explanation_en: The Bootstrap (primordial) ClassLoader is written in native code and loads the core Java classes. It is the root of the hierarchy, so it has no parent. Its child is the Platform/Extension loader, whose child is the Application/System loader, which has no child loaders by default.

Hindi overrides the default method greet(). Inside the override, Greeter.super.greet() calls the interface's default version, which returns "Hello". The call g.greet() runs Hindi's version at run time and returns "Namaste Hello".

question_en: Which statement about Java packages is TRUE?

options.en: Each package can contain only a single class or interface
An import statement copies the class code into the file
The java.lang package must always be imported explicitly
They prevent naming conflicts and provide controlled access

explanation_en: A package groups related classes, so two classes with the same name can live in different packages, and default/protected access is controlled at package level. import only lets you use short names; it copies no code. java.lang is imported automatically.

n is static, so one copy is shared by all objects; it starts at 0. Creating a and b calls the constructor twice (n = 2). The array c[3] creates three more objects, and the constructor runs for each one (n = 5). Output: 5.

question_en: In C++, what does the statement cin.ignore(100, '\n'); do?

options.en: Discards the last 100 characters typed before the '\n' character
Discards up to 100 input characters, stopping once '\n' is discarded
Reads 100 characters into a buffer, skipping only the '\n' character
Waits 100 milliseconds for the user to press the Enter key

explanation_en: istream::ignore(n, delim) extracts and throws away characters from the input stream. It stops after n characters or after the delimiter has been extracted, whichever comes first. It is often used to remove the leftover newline from the buffer.

T a; calls the default constructor: D. T b = a; makes a new object from an existing one, so the copy constructor runs: C. f(a) passes the object by value, so the parameter x is made with the copy constructor: C. Output: DCC.

question_en: In a C++ program, the statement cin >> age; is followed by getline(cin, name);, and name gets an empty string. Why?

options.en: getline cannot read any string that contains blank spaces
getline reads the newline that cin >> left in the input buffer
cin >> always clears the whole input buffer after reading
getline reads only from files and never from the keyboard

explanation_en: cin >> age reads the number but leaves the Enter key's '\n' in the buffer. getline reads up to the next '\n', finds it at once, and returns an empty string. Calling cin.ignore() before getline removes the leftover newline.

add(2, 3) has int arguments, so the int version runs and returns 2 + 3 = 5. add(2.0, 3.0) has double arguments, so the double version runs and returns 2.0 * 3.0 = 6.0. cout prints the double 6.0 as 6 by default. Output: 5 6.

subtopic: Pure virtual function and abstract class (C++)
question_en: In C++, a class becomes an abstract class when it:

options.en: Declares at least one pure virtual function (= 0)
Has no data members of its own
Is declared with the keyword abstract

explanation_en: A pure virtual function is declared like virtual void draw() = 0;. A class with at least one such function is abstract and cannot be instantiated. C++ has no abstract keyword; that keyword belongs to Java and C#.

final makes the reference arr constant: it cannot point to another array. The elements can still be changed, so arr[0] = 10 is legal. arr[0] + arr.length is int + int = 10 + 3 = 13 (numeric addition, not string joining).

question_en: In .NET, which component manages memory (garbage collection), security and exception handling while a program runs?
explanation_en: The CLR is the .NET execution engine and sits between the application and the operating system. It loads code, JIT-compiles it, and provides garbage collection, type safety, security and exception handling.

question_en: In .NET, the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler converts:

options.en: C# source code into MSIL code at compile time
MSIL (CIL) code into native machine code at run time
Native machine code back into MSIL code
VB.NET source code into equivalent C# code

explanation_en: .NET language compilers first produce MSIL (CIL), a CPU-independent intermediate code. When a method is first called, the CLR's JIT compiler turns that MSIL into native code for the current CPU.

question_en: The set of basic rules that a .NET language must follow so that its code can be used from other .NET languages is the:
explanation_en: The CLS is a subset of the CTS. It lists the rules that every CLS-compliant language and library must follow (for example, public members should not use unsigned types such as uint). This makes language interoperability possible: a VB.NET program can use a C# library.

question_en: In .NET, C# int and VB.NET Integer both map to System.Int32. Which component defines this common set of types?
explanation_en: The CTS defines how types are declared, used and managed in the runtime, so all .NET languages share one type system. Language keywords such as int (C#) and Integer (VB.NET) are aliases for the same CTS type, System.Int32.

question_en: Code that runs under the control of the CLR, which handles its memory and security, is called:
explanation_en: Managed code is executed by the CLR, which provides garbage collection, type checking and security. Unmanaged code, such as a C++ program compiled straight to machine code, runs directly on the operating system without CLR services.

question_en: In .NET, the Global Assembly Cache (GAC) is used to store:

options.en: Temporary files created by the JIT compiler at run time
Source code files of all installed .NET applications
Objects that the garbage collector has not yet freed
Strong-named assemblies shared by several applications

explanation_en: An assembly (.dll or .exe) is the unit of deployment in .NET and holds MSIL plus a manifest. A private assembly sits in its application's folder. A shared assembly must have a strong name and is installed in the GAC so that many applications can use it.

question_en: Which programming language, designed by Anders Hejlsberg, was released by Microsoft with .NET Framework 1.0 in 2002?
explanation_en: Microsoft released .NET Framework 1.0 in 2002, together with C# 1.0, a language designed by Anders Hejlsberg's team. Java is from Sun Microsystems (now Oracle), Kotlin is from JetBrains and Swift is from Apple.

question_en: Which statement about a static constructor in C# is TRUE?

options.en: It can be overloaded with different parameter lists
It must be called explicitly using the new keyword
It has no parameters and runs once, before the class is first used
It runs again each time a new object is created

explanation_en: A static constructor takes no parameters and no access modifier, and a class can have only one. The CLR calls it automatically, exactly once, before the first instance is created or any static member is used. It is used to initialise static data.

question_en: Which statement about a constructor in C# is TRUE?

options.en: It must always be declared with the return type void
It can be called only once in the whole program
A class is allowed to have only one constructor
It has the same name as its class and no return type

explanation_en: A C# constructor has the same name as the class and no return type, not even void. It runs automatically when an object is created with new. Constructors can be overloaded, and the compiler supplies a default one if none is written.

question_en: Which of the following is a value type in C#?
explanation_en: Value types (int, double, bool, char, enum and struct) hold their data directly, usually on the stack. class, interface, string, arrays and delegates are reference types: the variable holds a reference to an object on the managed heap.

question_en: In C#, the statement object o = 25; converts a value type into a reference type. This conversion is called:
explanation_en: Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap, so it can be treated as System.Object. The reverse, int n = (int)o;, is unboxing and needs an explicit cast.

question_en: In C#, a class member declared internal can be accessed:

options.en: Only in classes derived from it

explanation_en: internal limits access to the current assembly (the same .dll or .exe). private allows only the containing class, protected allows the class and its derived classes, and public allows any code. protected internal combines protected and internal.

question_en: Which C# collection stores key-value pairs with unique keys and compile-time type safety, as a generic replacement for Hashtable?
explanation_en: Hashtable (System.Collections) stores key-value pairs and finds a value by its unique key, but keys and values are just object. Dictionary<TKey, TValue> (System.Collections.Generic) does the same with type safety. List<T> and ArrayList are accessed by index, and Queue<T> is FIFO.

question_en: In VB.NET, which control lets the user select several options from a group at the same time?
explanation_en: Each CheckBox can be ticked or cleared on its own, so any number can be selected. RadioButtons in one group are mutually exclusive, so only one can be selected. A Label shows text and a TextBox takes typed input.

question_en: Which VB.NET control combines a text box with a drop-down list, so the user can pick an item or type a value?
explanation_en: A ComboBox is a text box with a drop-down list. A ListBox shows a list that is always visible and has no editable text area. A CheckBox is a single on/off option, and a PictureBox shows an image.

question_en: Which of the following is a valid single-line comment in Python?
explanation_en: In Python, # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. // is the floor-division operator in Python and a comment only in C, C++ and Java. /* */ is a C-style block comment, and <!-- --> is an HTML comment.

question_en: Which of the following is a valid identifier in Python?
explanation_en: An identifier may contain letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, and cannot be a keyword. _total2 follows these rules. 2total starts with a digit, total-marks contains a hyphen (the minus operator), and for is a keyword.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
print(chr(ord('a') - 32), ord('B') + 1)
```
explanation_en: ord('a') is 97, and 97 - 32 = 65; chr(65) is 'A'. ord('B') is 66, and 66 + 1 = 67, which stays an int because chr() is not applied. print separates the two values with a space: A 67.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
print(int("12") + float("3.5"), str(7) * 2)
```
explanation_en: int("12") is 12 and float("3.5") is 3.5; int + float gives the float 15.5. str(7) is the string "7", and multiplying a string by 2 repeats it: "77". Output: 15.5 77.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
print(17 // 5, 17 % 5, -17 // 5, 2 ** 3 ** 2)
```
explanation_en: 17 // 5 = 3 and 17 % 5 = 2. Floor division rounds toward minus infinity, so -17 // 5 = floor(-3.4) = -4. ** is right-associative: 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b, a is c)
```
explanation_en: == compares values: a and b hold equal lists, so True. is compares identity: a and b are two separate list objects, so a is b is False. c = a binds c to the same object, so a is c is True.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
s = "DSSSB2024"
print(s[2:6], s[-4:], s[::-3])
```
explanation_en: Indexes: D0 S1 S2 S3 B4 2(5) 0(6) 2(7) 4(8). s[2:6] takes indexes 2 to 5: SSB2. s[-4:] is the last four characters: 2024. s[::-3] starts at index 8 and moves back by 3: indexes 8, 5, 2 give 4, 2, S, so 42S.

subtopic: max() and min() on a string
question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
print(max("Delhi"), min("Delhi"))
```
explanation_en: max() and min() on a string compare Unicode (ASCII) values. D=68, e=101, l=108, h=104, i=105. The largest is 'l' (108). The smallest is the capital 'D' (68), because uppercase letters have smaller codes than lowercase ones.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
s = "  Delhi  "
print("[" + s.strip() + "]", len(s.rstrip()))
```
explanation_en: strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace, giving "Delhi", so the first part prints [Delhi]. rstrip() removes only the trailing spaces, giving "  Delhi": 2 spaces + 5 letters = 7 characters.

subtopic: split() with and without a separator
question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
print("a,b,,c".split(","), len("a b  c".split()))
```
explanation_en: With an explicit separator, split(",") cuts at every comma, so the two commas side by side give an empty string: ['a', 'b', '', 'c']. With no argument, split() splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty pieces, so "a b  c" gives ['a', 'b', 'c'], of length 3.

question_en: For a Python string s, what happens when the substring is NOT found by s.find(sub) and by s.index(sub)?

options.en: Both return -1 when sub is not found
Both return None when sub is not found

explanation_en: Both methods return the lowest index where sub starts. They differ only when sub is absent: find() returns -1, while index() raises ValueError: substring not found.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
L = [1, 2]
L.append([3, 4])
L.extend([5, 6])
print(len(L), L)
```
explanation_en: append() adds its argument as one element, so the whole list [3, 4] becomes one item: [1, 2, [3, 4]]. extend() adds each element of the iterable separately: [1, 2, [3, 4], 5, 6]. That is 5 elements.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
L = [3, 1, 2]
x = L.sort()
print(x, L)
```
explanation_en: list.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None, like append(), extend(), insert(), remove() and reverse(). So x is None, and L itself is now [1, 2, 3]. Use sorted(L) when a new sorted list is wanted.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = a[:]
b.append(4)
c.append(5)
print(a, len(c))
```
explanation_en: b = a makes b another name (alias) for the same list, so b.append(4) changes a to [1, 2, 3, 4]. a[:] makes a new copy, so c is a separate list [1, 2, 3], and appending 5 to it does not affect a. len(c) is 4.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
L = [10, 20, 30, 40]
L.insert(1, 15)
L.pop()
L.remove(20)
print(L)
```
explanation_en: insert(1, 15) puts 15 at index 1: [10, 15, 20, 30, 40]. pop() with no argument removes the last item (40): [10, 15, 20, 30]. remove(20) deletes the first element equal to 20: [10, 15, 30].

subtopic: List slicing with a negative step
question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
L = list(range(10))
print(L[8:2:-2], L[-3:])
```
explanation_en: L is [0, 1, ..., 9]. L[8:2:-2] starts at index 8 and moves back by 2 while the index is greater than 2 (the stop is excluded): 8, 6, 4. L[-3:] gives the last three elements in their normal order: [7, 8, 9].

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
t = (5)
u = (5,)
print(type(t).__name__, type(u).__name__, len(u))
```
explanation_en: Brackets alone do not make a tuple; (5) is just the int 5 in brackets. The comma makes the tuple, so (5,) is a one-element tuple. len(u) is 1. Output: int tuple 1.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
t = ("x", 10, "y", 20, "z")
print(t[1::2], t[-1], t.index("y"))
```
explanation_en: t[1::2] starts at index 1 and takes every second element: indexes 1 and 3 give (10, 20). Slicing a tuple returns a tuple. t[-1] is the last element, z. t.index("y") gives the position of "y", which is 2.

subtopic: Tuple immutability with a mutable element
question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
t = (1, [2, 3])
t[1].append(4)
print(t, len(t))
```
explanation_en: A tuple's own slots cannot be reassigned, but an object stored in a slot can change if it is mutable. t[1] is a list, and append() changes that list in place without assigning anything to the tuple, so there is no error. t becomes (1, [2, 3, 4]) and still has 2 elements.

question_en: Which pair of methods is available on a Python tuple object?
explanation_en: A tuple is immutable, so it has only the two methods that do not change it: count(x) and index(x). append, extend, sort and reverse are list methods, and add/remove are set methods (list also has remove).

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
s = {3, 1, 3, 2, 1}
s.add(2)
s.add(4)
print(len(s), sorted(s))
```
explanation_en: A set keeps only unique elements, so {3, 1, 3, 2, 1} is {1, 2, 3}. add(2) changes nothing because 2 is already there; add(4) adds 4. The set has 4 elements, and sorted() returns them as a sorted list: [1, 2, 3, 4].

& is intersection (common elements): {3, 4}. a - b keeps elements of a that are not in b: {1, 2}. a | b is the union {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, of length 5. ^ is symmetric difference (in exactly one set): {1, 2, 5}.

question_en: Which of the following CANNOT be used as a key in a Python dictionary?
explanation_en: Dictionary keys must be hashable, which in practice means immutable. Strings, numbers and tuples of immutable items can be keys. A list is mutable and unhashable, so {[1, 2]: 'x'} raises TypeError. Values can be of any type.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
d = {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'a': 3}
print(d, len(d))
```
explanation_en: Keys are unique. When a key is repeated, the later value replaces the earlier one, but the key keeps its first position. So 'a' stays first with value 3, and the dictionary has 2 items.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
d = {'x': 10}
print(d.get('y'), d.get('y', 0), d.setdefault('z', 5), len(d))
```
explanation_en: get('y') returns None for a missing key instead of raising KeyError. get('y', 0) returns the default 0, and neither call adds a key. setdefault('z', 5) inserts 'z': 5 because 'z' is missing and returns 5. d now has 2 keys.

question_en: In Python 3.7 and later, what does d.popitem() remove from a dictionary d?

options.en: The pair with the smallest key

explanation_en: From Python 3.7, dictionaries keep insertion order, and popitem() removes and returns the most recently inserted (key, value) pair (LIFO order). It raises KeyError if the dictionary is empty. pop(key) removes a chosen key.

A loop's else block runs only if the loop ends without break. The for loop counts 3 and 7 (count = 2), then breaks at 10, so its else is skipped and count stays 2. The while loop ends normally when i becomes 3, so its else runs and i = 30.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
def f(a, b=2, c=3):
    return a + b * c
print(f(1), f(1, c=1), f(1, 4))
```
explanation_en: f(1): a=1, b=2, c=3, so 1 + 2*3 = 7. f(1, c=1): b keeps its default 2, so 1 + 2*1 = 3. f(1, 4): the second positional argument sets b=4 and c=3, so 1 + 4*3 = 13.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items
add(1)
print(add(2), add(3, []))
```
explanation_en: A default value is created once, when def runs, and is shared by all calls that use it. add(1) makes the default list [1]; add(2) uses the same list, giving [1, 2]. add(3, []) is given a new empty list, so it returns [3].

*nums collects all positional arguments into a tuple. stats(4, 5, 6) returns len 3 and sum 15. Writing return a, b returns a tuple, which prints as (3, 15). stats() returns (0, 0), whose type is tuple.

question_en: The statement import pandas stops with ModuleNotFoundError, a subclass of ImportError. What does this mean?

options.en: The pandas module was found but contains a syntax error
pandas was imported successfully but is an old version
The program file was not saved with a .py extension
Python could not find the pandas module in its search path

explanation_en: ImportError (and its subclass ModuleNotFoundError) is raised when Python cannot find or load the module named in an import statement. The usual cause is that the library is not installed in the current environment, which pip install pandas fixes.

question_en: After the statement import math as m, which of the following calls works?
explanation_en: import math as m binds the module only to the name m, so its functions are used as m.sqrt(25), which gives 5.0. The name math is not defined, and sqrt alone would need from math import sqrt.

question_en: Which file mode opens a file for both reading and appending, creates the file if it does not exist, and sends every write to the end of the file?
explanation_en: a+ opens for appending and reading, creates a missing file, and always writes at the end, keeping the old data. r+ is read/write with the pointer at the start and needs an existing file. w+ is write/read but empties the file first. rb is read-only binary.

question_en: Which file mode opens a file for writing and reading but first erases any existing contents?
explanation_en: w and w+ truncate an existing file to zero length, or create it if it is missing. w+ also allows reading. r+ keeps the contents and starts at the beginning, a+ keeps the contents and writes at the end, and rb only reads in binary.

subtopic: Mode that needs an existing file
question_en: Which of the following modes raises FileNotFoundError when the file does not already exist?
explanation_en: The read modes (r, r+, rb, rb+) need an existing file and raise FileNotFoundError otherwise. The modes w, w+, a and a+ create the file if it is missing.

question_en: Which of the following is normally handled as a binary file (opened with a mode such as 'rb') in Python?
explanation_en: Text files (.txt, .csv, .py, .html) hold readable characters stored line by line and are opened in text mode. Images, audio, video and .exe files hold raw bytes that are not text, so they are opened in binary mode ('rb', 'wb'), and read() returns bytes.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("one\ntwo\nthree\n")
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    a = f.readline()
    b = f.read(3)
    c = f.readlines()
print(repr(a), b, len(c))
```
explanation_en:
readline() reads one line including its newline, so a is 'one
'. read(3) reads the next 3 characters: two. The pointer is now just before the newline after two, so readlines() returns ['
', 'three
'], a list of length 2.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
with open("s.txt", "w") as f:
    n = f.write("PYTHON")
with open("s.txt") as f:
    f.seek(2)
    x = f.read(3)
    print(n, x, f.tell())
```
explanation_en: write() returns the number of characters written: 6. seek(2) moves the file pointer to offset 2, which is the character T (P=0, Y=1, T=2). read(3) reads THO, and the pointer moves on to offset 5, which tell() reports.

question_en: What is the main advantage of opening a file with with open('a.txt') as f: ?

options.en: The file is opened in both read and write mode together
The whole file is loaded into memory before any reading
The file is closed automatically, even if an error occurs
The file is locked so no other program can open it

explanation_en: with uses the file object as a context manager. When the block ends, normally or because of an exception, the file's close() is called automatically. This avoids leaving files open and losing data that has not been written yet.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("12")
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("34")
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("56")
with open("log.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
```
explanation_en: The first 'w' writes 12. The second 'w' truncates the file, so 12 is lost and the file holds 34. 'a' keeps the contents and adds 56 at the end, giving 3456. The final read prints 3456.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import csv
with open("marks.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["roll", "marks"])
    w.writerow([1, 95])
with open("marks.csv", newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.reader(f))
print(rows[1], len(rows))
```
explanation_en: The file has two lines: roll,marks and 1,95. csv.reader returns each line as a list of strings; it does not convert numbers. So rows[1] is ['1', '95'], and rows has 2 rows, the header included.

question_en: Which csv.writer method writes every row of a list of lists in a single call?
explanation_en: writerow(row) writes one row, and writerows(rows) writes every row of an iterable of rows. writelines() is a method of ordinary file objects that writes strings without CSV formatting. There is no writeall() method.

subtopic: Pandas Series - label and position access
question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=['a', 'b', 'c'])
print(s['b'] + s.iloc[2], len(s))
```
explanation_en: A Series is a one-dimensional labelled array. s['b'] picks by label and gives 20; s.iloc[2] picks by position (0-based) and gives 30. 20 + 30 = 50, and the Series has 3 elements.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['A', 'B', 'C'], 'marks': [70, 85, 90]})
print(df.shape, df['marks'].max())
```
explanation_en: Each dictionary key becomes a column and each list holds that column's values. There are 3 rows and 2 columns, so shape is (rows, columns) = (3, 2). df['marks'].max() is 90.

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([5, 6, 7, 8], index=[1, 2, 3, 4])
print(s.loc[1:3].sum(), s.iloc[1:3].sum())
```
explanation_en: loc slices by label and includes the end label, so s.loc[1:3] takes labels 1, 2 and 3: 5 + 6 + 7 = 18. iloc slices by position and excludes the end, like a Python list, so s.iloc[1:3] takes positions 1 and 2: 6 + 7 = 13.

subtopic: Pandas concat along axis 0 and axis 1
question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
df1 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [5, 6], 'B': [7, 8]})
print(pd.concat([df1, df2]).shape, pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1).shape)
```
explanation_en: pd.concat() joins along axis 0 by default, stacking the rows: 2 + 2 = 4 rows and the same 2 columns, so (4, 2). With axis=1 the frames are placed side by side: 2 rows and 2 + 2 = 4 columns, so (2, 4).

subtopic: Pandas merge - inner join on a key
question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
left = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3], 'name': ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Gita']})
right = pd.DataFrame({'id': [2, 3, 4], 'marks': [50, 60, 70]})
m = pd.merge(left, right, on='id')
print(len(m), list(m.columns))
```
explanation_en: pd.merge() joins two DataFrames like a database join, with how='inner' by default. Only id values found in both frames (2 and 3) are kept, so there are 2 rows. The key column id appears once, followed by the other columns: ['id', 'name', 'marks'].

question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'roll': [101, 102, 103], 'name': ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Gita']})
df2 = df.set_index('roll')
print(df2.loc[102, 'name'], df2.shape)
```
explanation_en: set_index('roll') returns a new DataFrame whose row labels are the roll values, and roll is no longer a data column. So df2 has 3 rows and 1 column, shape (3, 1). df2.loc[102, 'name'] looks up the row labelled 102: Ravi.

question_en: When called without an argument, df.head() on a pandas DataFrame returns:
explanation_en: head(n=5) returns the first n rows, and n defaults to 5. tail() returns the last 5 rows in the same way. The column names come from df.columns, and the size from df.shape.

question_en: In pandas, selecting one column of a DataFrame with df['marks'] returns an object of type:
explanation_en: A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labelled table, and each of its columns is a one-dimensional Series that shares the DataFrame's index. df['marks'] returns that Series. df[['marks']], with a list of names, returns a DataFrame.
